subject: Cooking
title: Herbes de Provence: Sun-Dried Memory
description: A 60-second lesson on Herbes de Provence: Sun-Dried Memory.

hook.text: Herbes de Provence smells like a summer afternoon in southern France — lavender, thyme, and warm stone.

buildup.text: The blend typically includes thyme, rosemary, oregano, marjoram, and savory — all native to Provence.

discovery.text: Lavender is the controversial ingredient — traditional Provençal cooks rarely used it in daily cooking.

twist.text: The 'official' blend was actually commercialized in the 1970s for export — locals found it amusing.

climax.text: Authentic or not, the blend captures Mediterranean terroir in a way no single herb can.

punchline.text: Some traditions are invented. That doesn't make them less delicious.

quiz.question: Which herb in herbes de Provence is considered a non-traditional addition?

details.summary: Herbes de Provence is a blend of sun-dried herbs from southern France including thyme, rosemary, oregano, savory, and marjoram, sometimes with lavender. The blend captures the aromatic landscape of Provence and pairs with grilled meats, roasted vegetables, and olive oil-based dishes.
details.whyItMatters: This blend shows how regional geography shapes cuisine. The herbs that grow wild in Provence's rocky, sunny hillsides became the signature flavor of its cooking tradition.
takeaways: Traditional herbs include thyme, rosemary, oregano, and savory
Lavender is a modern addition not in all traditional versions
Best used with olive oil, grilled meats, and roasted vegetables

faq.question: Does authentic herbes de Provence include lavender?
faq.answer: Traditional Provençal cooking rarely used lavender in savory dishes. Commercial blends marketed to tourists and export markets added it for Provençal mystique. Authentic versions focus on thyme, savory, rosemary, oregano, and marjoram. Lavender can overwhelm if used heavily.

faq.question: What is the best way to use herbes de Provence?
faq.answer: Rub it on meat with olive oil before grilling or roasting. Add it to ratatouille and other vegetable dishes. Mix it into bread dough or focaccia. Sprinkle on goat cheese with olive oil. The dried herbs bloom in fat and heat, releasing their essential oils.
